title: Driving Neurons to Test What They Cause
endLine: Stimulation tests cause only as finely as it drives distinct neurons.

scenes.tts: A neuron fires faster before a choice, but does it cause it? A monkey watches moving dots and moves its eyes to answer. On average, a neuron toward the top and back of its brain fires faster and faster. Yet recording spikes alone cannot prove that region decides.
scenes.caption: A neuron fires faster before a choice, but does it cause it? A monkey watches moving dots and moves its eyes to answer. On average, a neuron toward the top and back of its brain fires faster and faster. Yet recording spikes alone cannot prove that region decides.
scenes.visual: Establish the film's one carried world (schematic, filling most of the frame height): on the left, a row of distinct neuron groups with a passive recording probe above one glowing group; on the right, a perception and behaviour window showing a drifting cloud of moving dots. As narration opens, spikes stream faster along the active fibre (schematic, an average trace) and an eye-movement arrow appears on the right, then a bold question mark pulses over the link between neuron and choice, labelled "Causes choice?" (schematic).
scenes.narration: A neuron fires faster before a choice, but does it cause it? A monkey watches moving dots and moves its eyes to answer. On average, a neuron toward the top and back of its brain fires faster and faster. Yet recording spikes alone cannot prove that region decides.

scenes.visual: The same schematic neural map and gently drifting spikes dim softly in the background while the title "Driving Neurons to Test What They Cause" sits centered in crisp full-opacity type.

scenes.tts: To test cause, you stop only listening and activate neurons yourself. Small currents through electrodes, or magnetic pulses, trigger spikes directly. Every sense ends in the same currency: trains of identical spikes. Spike rate and the number of active fibres say how much.
scenes.caption: To test cause, you stop only listening and activate neurons yourself. Small currents through electrodes, or magnetic pulses, trigger spikes directly. Every sense ends in the same currency: trains of identical spikes. Spike rate and the number of active fibres say how much.
scenes.visual: In the same carried neural map (schematic), the passive recording probe transforms into a stimulating electrode delivering a crisp current pulse while a soft magnetic-pulse arc sweeps from above. Identical spike pulses race along the activated fibres; raising the pulse rate and recruiting neighbouring fibres lights "How much" in the right readout window.
scenes.narration: To test cause, you stop only listening and activate neurons yourself. Small currents through electrodes, or magnetic pulses, trigger spikes directly. Every sense ends in the same currency: trains of identical spikes. Spike rate and the number of active fibres say how much.

scenes.tts: A cochlear implant uses that code, threading electrode contacts into the cochlea, the inner ear's hearing coil. It skips damaged hair cells, the ear's sensors, and excites the auditory nerve directly. Speech often sounds harsh or robotic at first. Even twenty-two contacts do not carry all the information normal hearing does.
scenes.caption: A cochlear implant uses that code, threading electrode contacts into the cochlea, the inner ear's hearing coil. It skips damaged hair cells, the ear's sensors, and excites the auditory nerve directly. Speech often sounds harsh or robotic at first. Even 22 contacts do not carry all the information normal hearing does.
scenes.visual: The same horizontal neuron-group map curves smoothly into a schematic cochlea strip with faded damaged hair cells bypassed along one edge; a thin array of 22 small electrode contacts slides into place along the probe rail beside the auditory nerve fibres. Small current pulses jump directly into the nerve as the right perception window shows a jagged, robotic sound waveform labelled "At first" (schematic).
scenes.narration: A cochlear implant uses that code, threading electrode contacts into the cochlea, the inner ear's hearing coil. It skips damaged hair cells, the ear's sensors, and excites the auditory nerve directly. Speech often sounds harsh or robotic at first. Even 22 contacts do not carry all the information normal hearing does.

scenes.tts: In the eye, an epiretinal grid sits on the retina's inner surface. Asked to draw what one electrode made them see, users often drew elongated or distorted shapes, not a dot. Current spread blurs neighbouring groups together; current reaching wrong neurons misplaces the signal. Stimulation delivers detail only as far as it drives distinct groups, each in the right place.
scenes.caption: In the eye, an epiretinal grid sits on the retina's inner surface. Asked to draw what one electrode made them see, users often drew elongated or distorted shapes, not a dot. scenes.visual: The electrode array flattens into a schematic epiretinal grid resting on the retina's inner surface above the same neuron-group map. One single contact lights up; its glowing electric field expands outward across neighbouring neuron groups, and in the right perception window a crisp target dot stretches into an elongated, distorted streak. As the guiding idea is spoken, distinct coloured boundaries briefly clarify around separated neuron groups (schematic).

scenes.tts: Try a toy case: suppose twenty-two contacts lie along about sixteen millimetres. Give each contact's electric field an illustrative width of one point seven five millimetres. Roughly how many separate channels fit before fields overlap?
scenes.caption: Try a toy case: suppose 22 contacts lie along about 16 mm. Give each contact's electric field an illustrative width of 1.75 mm. Roughly how many separate channels fit before fields overlap?
scenes.visual: The grid transforms back into a toy array of 22 contacts along a 16 mm bar labelled "toy case" over the same neural map. One contact's electric-field halo widens to a bracket labelled "1.75 mm (illustrative)", while the right window displays the large question "How many separate channels?" (schematic field width, computed scale bar).
scenes.narration: Try a toy case: suppose 22 contacts lie along about 16 mm. Give each contact's electric field an illustrative width of 1.75 mm. Roughly how many separate channels fit before fields overlap?

scenes.visual: Hold the exact 16 mm bar with 22 contacts, the 1.75 mm illustrative field bracket, and the question "How many separate channels?" on screen during the silent pause, with gentle ambient shimmer in the electric-field halo.

scenes.tts: Length divided by field width gives a rough channel count. Sixteen millimetres divided by one point seven five millimetres is about nine, far fewer than twenty-two. Overlapping fields excite overlapping neuron groups, called channel interaction. This is a toy picture, not a prediction: real fields fade gradually.
scenes.caption: Length divided by field width gives a rough channel count. 16 mm ÷ 1.75 mm ≈ 9, far fewer than 22. Overlapping fields excite overlapping neuron groups, called channel interaction. This is a toy picture, not a prediction: real fields fade gradually.
scenes.visual: Above the same 16 mm bar, the formula "Length ÷ field width" appears, then updates piece by piece as spoken: "16 mm ÷ 1.75 mm ≈ 9" (computed) while 9 field circles pack across the bar beneath the crowded 22 contacts. Overlapping zones brighten with the label "Channel interaction", then their hard edges soften into fading gradients beside the tag "Toy packing — fields fade gradually" (schematic gradients).
scenes.narration: Length divided by field width gives a rough channel count. 16 mm ÷ 1.75 mm ≈ 9, far fewer than 22. Overlapping fields excite overlapping neuron groups, called channel interaction. This is a toy picture, not a prediction: real fields fade gradually.

scenes.tts: So counting contacts misleads; you must measure what the user can tell apart. No single channel count fits every listener. Neural survival, the distance from contacts to neurons, and the array's reach all matter. Many users also understand much more after weeks to months.
scenes.caption: So counting contacts misleads; you must measure what the user can tell apart. No single channel count fits every listener. Neural survival, the distance from contacts to neurons, and the array's reach all matter. Many users also understand much more after weeks to months.
scenes.visual: Still on the same cochlear array and neural map (schematic), a "22 contacts" badge fades out as a "Measured: what the user tells apart" gauge rises on the right. Along the map, a few nerve fibres dim (neural survival), the array shifts subtly farther and shallower (distance and reach), and a soft "Weeks to months" bar sweeps forward as speech clarity improves.
scenes.narration: So counting contacts misleads; you must measure what the user can tell apart. No single channel count fits every listener. Neural survival, the distance from contacts to neurons, and the array's reach all matter. Many users also understand much more after weeks to months.

scenes.tts: Switching channels on and off tested this directly in listeners. In 2020, Berg and colleagues tested eighteen adult implant users. Speech recognition reached a plateau, no longer rising, at eight to ten channels.
scenes.caption: Switching channels on and off tested this directly in listeners. In 2020, Berg and colleagues tested 18 adult implant users. Speech recognition reached a plateau, no longer rising, at 8 to 10 channels.
scenes.visual: Active contacts toggle on and off along the carried cochlear array while the right window draws a clean schematic curve anchored to the reported numbers for "Berg and colleagues, 2020 (18 adults)": speech recognition climbs and then levels off across a highlighted "8–10 channels" plateau.
scenes.narration: Switching channels on and off tested this directly in listeners. In 2020, Berg and colleagues tested 18 adult implant users. Speech recognition reached a plateau, no longer rising, at 8 to 10 channels.

scenes.tts: Yet one plateau does not mean extra contacts do nothing. In 2017, Schvartz-Leyzac, Zwolan and Pfingst cut active electrodes from twenty to eight in seven adults. Their speech-in-noise threshold worsened: speech had to be louder relative to background noise to be understood.
scenes.caption: Yet one plateau does not mean extra contacts do nothing. In 2017, Schvartz-Leyzac, Zwolan and Pfingst cut active electrodes from 20 to 8 in seven adults. Their speech-in-noise threshold worsened: speech had to be louder relative to background noise to be understood.
scenes.visual: On the same carried cochlear array, active contacts step down from 20 to 8 while background noise static rises in the right window; a schematic comparison for "Schvartz-Leyzac, Zwolan and Pfingst, 2017 (seven adults)" shows the "Speech-in-noise threshold" shifting worse, lifting speech higher above background noise.
scenes.narration: Yet one plateau does not mean extra contacts do nothing. In 2017, Schvartz-Leyzac, Zwolan and Pfingst cut active electrodes from 20 to 8 in seven adults. Their speech-in-noise threshold worsened: speech had to be louder relative to background noise to be understood.

scenes.tts: Helping in noise does not mean every contact acts independently. Whether probing a decision or restoring a sense, stimulation is only as precise as the distinct neurons it drives. Behaviour then shows what those neurons do.
scenes.caption: Helping in noise does not mean every contact acts independently. Whether probing a decision or restoring a sense, stimulation is only as precise as the distinct neurons it drives. Behaviour then shows what those neurons do.
scenes.visual: The summary plots recede back into the carried neural map (schematic). Overlapping electric halos tighten into distinct, cleanly separated active neuron groups along the map while the right readout clears, briefly echoing both the opening choice arrow and sensory readout in harmony.
scenes.narration: Helping in noise does not mean every contact acts independently. Whether probing a decision or restoring a sense, stimulation is only as precise as the distinct neurons it drives. Behaviour then shows what those neurons do.

scenes.visual: The carried schematic neural map with gently shimmering separated neuron groups dims behind the centered end card: "Stimulation tests cause only as finely as it drives distinct neurons."
